title: Stack: matching and the minimum
sub: Valid Parentheses and Min Stack: the last one opened closes first, and the minimum lives next to each element
cards/0/title: The problem and the stack signals
cards/0/body:
Valid Parentheses (LeetCode #20). Given a string s of the characters ()[]{}, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴. It is valid if every opening bracket is closed by a bracket of the same type and the closings come in the right order: "([]{})" — yes, "([)]" — no, "(()" — no.

The key observation: you can only close the bracket that was opened last. Last in, first out: that is a stack. Stack<T> in .NET is an array whose end is the top; Push, Pop and Peek are O(1).

Stack signals in a problem statement:

1. Nesting and matching: brackets, tags, begin … end blocks.
2. “Undo the last one”, “go back”: undo, a Back button.
3. An element waits until something to its right “closes” it, and the nearest one does: the last open bracket, the next greater element to the right (that is the next lesson).
4. A recursion has to become a loop — an explicit stack instead of the call stack.
cards/0/code:
IsValid("([]{})"); // true
IsValid("([)]");   // false: ")" arrives while "[" was opened last
IsValid("(()");    // false: one "(" is never closed
cards/1/q: Which problems have a stack as the natural solution? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Check that markup tags are nested correctly:
cards/1/options/1: Evaluate “3 4 + 2 *”: an operator takes the last two numbers and puts the result back
cards/1/options/2: The Back button in a game menu returns to the previous screen
cards/1/options/3: Hand out jobs to workers in the order they arrived
cards/1/options/4: Find out whether some number appears in the array twice
cards/1/explain: Tags are the same matching as brackets (signal 1). In the expression an operator takes the last two numbers — the top of the stack — and the result goes back there (Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, #150). Back returns to the screen opened last (signal 2). Jobs in arrival order are first in, first out: a queue. A repeated number is “have I seen this?”, a hash set from unit 2.
cards/2/title: Naive solutions and where they break
cards/2/body:
Cut out pairs. While the string contains "()", "[]" or "{}", remove them; a valid string disappears completely. It is correct, but every Replace is an O(n) pass and a new string, and there can be up to n/2 rounds: on "((((…))))" each round removes one pair. That is O(n²): for n = 10⁴, up to 5000 rounds over 10⁴ characters, on the order of 5·10⁷ operations and thousands of new strings of up to 20 KB thrown to the garbage collector.

A counter. For a single bracket type a number open is enough: +1 on (, −1 on ), never go negative, end at zero. That is O(n) with O(1) memory. But three counters for three types cannot see order: on "([)]" each one honestly returns to zero and never goes negative, yet the string is invalid — ) tries to close [.

We need to remember not how many brackets are open, but which one was opened last.
cards/3/q: A solution with three counters: one per type, +1 on an opening bracket, −1 on a closing one, never negative, all zero at the end. What does it return on "[(])"?
cards/3/options/0: true, while the correct answer is false: counters do not remember which bracket was opened last
cards/3/options/1: false: the square-bracket counter goes negative
cards/3/options/2: true, and that is correct: every bracket is closed by its own type
cards/3/explain: [ and ( add +1 to their counters, ] and ) bring them back to zero — nothing went negative, the check passes. But ] arrives while ( is the last one opened, so it is too early to close [. Order is lost — you need a stack.
cards/3/wrong/1: Square brackets: [ gives +1, ] gives −1 — zero, not negative. The counters do not see that ( is open between them.
cards/3/wrong/2: The types match, the order does not: ] closes [ while ( is still open inside it.
cards/4/title: The idea: a stack of open brackets
cards/4/body:
Walk the string. Push every opening bracket. A closing bracket must match the top: pop the top and compare it with the expected pair.

Invariant: the stack holds the brackets that are open and not yet closed, in the order they were opened, with the last one on top. That is why a closing bracket is compared with the top only, not with the whole stack.

The string is invalid in three cases: the top does not match ("([)]"); the stack is empty when a closing bracket arrives ("())"); the string ends with a non-empty stack ("(()"). The second case also matters because Pop on an empty Stack<T> throws InvalidOperationException — check Count first.

A “closing → opening” dictionary answers with a single TryGetValue whether this is a closing bracket and hands you its pair. Time O(n), memory O(n) in the worst case "((((". Early exit: a string of odd length can never be valid.
cards/4/flow/2: closing: stack empty or Pop() ≠ pair → false
cards/4/flow/3: end of string: is the stack empty?
cards/5/task: Step through "{[]}([)]". The rig stops twice and asks what the code does with the next bracket: look only at the top of the stack.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: return false: the stack still holds a bracket
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: “[]” has already closed. Now “}” arrives. What does the code do?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: After popping “[” the top is “{” again — the pair for “}”. Pop it, and the stack is empty. A non-empty stack is an error only at the end of the string, not in the middle.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: pop: there is a “(” somewhere in the stack
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: The stack holds “(” and “[”, with “[” on top. Now “)” arrives. What does the code do?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: “)” can only close the last open bracket, and the last one opened is “[”. The “(” deeper down does not help: closing it before “[” would break the nesting. Pop gives “[” ≠ “(”, the answer is false.
cards/6/q: On "(()" this code returns true. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: The loop catches two of the three cases: a mismatched top and a closing bracket on an empty stack. The third — opening brackets that were never closed — is visible only after the loop. On "(()" one “(” stays in the stack, yet the code says true. It must be return stack.Count == 0.
cards/7/title: Min Stack: the minimum next to each element
cards/7/body:
Min Stack (LeetCode #155). A stack with Push, Pop, Top and GetMin, each in O(1). Values span the whole int range, Pop, Top and GetMin are only called on a non-empty stack, up to 3·10⁴ calls.

Naively: GetMin by scanning — O(n). Or a single min field: easy to update on Push, but if Pop removes the minimum itself, the previous one cannot be recovered without a scan.

The idea. The minimum of the stack depends only on what lies below the top, and what lies below an element does not change while that element is in the stack. So the minimum can be computed once on insertion and stored next to the element: a pair (val, min), where min is the minimum of this element and everything below it. Pop removes the pair — and the minimum “rolls back” by itself. Stack<(int val, int min)> stores the tuple struct directly in the array: no boxing, no object per element.

The two-stack variant: the values plus a separate stack of minimums that only receives “records”. The condition is x <= mins.Peek(), not <: otherwise a second copy of the minimum never reaches mins, and the first Pop of a two removes the minimum while the other two is still in the stack. Memory: pairs always take 2n numbers, two stacks take n plus the number of records (on descending input, the same 2n).
cards/8/q: Assemble Min Stack on (value, minimum) pairs.
cards/8/explain: Empty stack: the minimum is the element itself. Otherwise it is the smaller of the new value and the minimum of everything below — which is already stored in the pair on top: stack.Peek().min. Comparing with stack.Peek().val is wrong — that is only the top element, not the minimum below it. Push (val, min) in the order the tuple fields are named.
cards/9/task: Step through push 4, 2, 2, 5, followed by a mix of pop and getMin. The rig stops twice before a pop and asks which minimum ends up on top.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: The stack holds (4, 4), (2, 2), (2, 2). Pop removes one of the twos. What is the minimum on the new top?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: Each two carries its own minimum. The upper one is gone — below it is (2, 2): the minimum is still 2, because the other two is still in the stack. The two-stack variant with x < mins.Peek() would fail here: the second two never reached mins, and this pop would take the minimum with it.
cards/9/goal/asks/1/q: Left: (4, 4), (2, 2). Pop removes the last two. What is the minimum on the new top?
cards/9/goal/asks/1/explain: Below the two is (4, 4): when 4 was pushed the minimum was 4, and it did not change while 4 stayed in the stack. Nothing is recomputed — the minimum rolled back by itself, O(1).
cards/10/title: In a game: a screen stack and undo/redo
cards/10/body:
A UI screen stack. Main menu → settings → “Reset progress?”. Opening a screen is Push and show it; Back (a button, Escape, the Android system back) is Pop and show the top again. A popup over a screen is a stack element too: the screen below stays visible but takes no input. “How would you build menu navigation?” at a Unity interview is exactly this.

Undo and redo are two stacks of commands. A player or level-editor action is an object with Do and Undo. Run it — push it onto undo. Undo — pop from undo, roll it back, push onto redo. Redo — the other way round. A new action clears redo: history has branched, and the old “forward” is no longer reachable.

Stack<T> cannot cap the history at, say, a hundred steps: there is no way to drop the oldest entry from the bottom. For that you use a fixed-capacity ring buffer (like the deque from the window unit), where a new entry overwrites the oldest. Unity’s built-in Undo.RecordObject exists only in the editor — in the game you write the history yourself.
cards/10/deep:
Inside Stack<T>. The fields are an array _array, a size _size and a version counter _version. The parameterless constructor allocates no array; the first Push creates one for 4 elements, then capacity doubles — Push is amortized O(1). For reference types (and structs containing references) Pop clears the freed slot so the collector can reclaim the object; the array itself never shrinks — Clear() keeps the capacity, TrimExcess() gives the excess back. foreach goes from the top to the bottom, and modifying the stack during enumeration throws InvalidOperationException. TryPop and TryPeek exist since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity since 2021.2.

Without the heap. For brackets, Span<char> st = s.Length <= 1024 ? stackalloc char[s.Length] : new char[s.Length]; plus a top index top is enough: push is st[top++] = c, pop is st[--top]. The threshold is there because the thread stack is limited (often just 1 MB). Burst has no managed Stack<T>: use a NativeArray<T> of the right capacity and the same top index.

Min Stack with O(1) extra memory. Keep one min field and push the difference x − min taken before updating the minimum. A negative difference means “this element became the new minimum”, and on Pop the previous minimum is restored as min − diff. The difference of two ints from the full range does not fit in an int — the stack has to hold long, so in bytes it barely beats the pairs. At an interview this answers “can you do it without a second stack?”, not the default solution.
cards/11/q: Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: The player did A, B, C, pressed Undo twice and then did D. Now Redo brings nothing back
cards/11/options/1: Two-stack Min Stack with x < mins.Peek(): after push 2, push 2, pop, GetMin returns 2
cards/11/options/2: stack.Pop() on an empty Stack<int> returns 0
cards/11/options/3: Stack<(int val, int min)> does not create a heap object on every Push
cards/11/options/4: Valid Parentheses: a string of odd length can be rejected right away
cards/11/explain: D is a new action, it clears redo: the undone B and C can no longer be redone. With < the second two never reached mins, popping a two removed the only record, and mins.Peek() on an empty stack throws — while the answer should be 2. Pop on an empty Stack<T> throws InvalidOperationException rather than returning default. The (int, int) tuple is a struct stored directly in the stack’s array. Every bracket needs a pair, and with an odd length one is left without it.
cards/12/q: You are solving Valid Parentheses out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: only the characters ()[]{}, can the string be empty, what is the length
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive approach: cut out pairs while you can — O(n²) and string garbage; counters cannot see order
cards/12/items/2: Idea: only the last open bracket can be closed — a stack of open brackets
cards/12/items/3: Write the code, stating the invariant: the stack holds open, unclosed brackets, the last one on top
cards/12/items/4: Run "([)]" and "(()": a mismatched top and a non-empty stack at the end
cards/12/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(n) memory in the worst case "(((("
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: a closing bracket on an empty stack, odd length
cards/12/explain: Agree on the problem, name the baseline and why it is bad, then the idea and the code with its invariant, a run on examples that catch two different errors, and finally the complexity and edge cases.
